title: Tell No One ("Ne Le Dis a Personne")
full_review:
"Tell No One" ("Ne Le Dis a Personne") (Music Box) is an absorbing mystery thriller, set in Paris, about Alexandre Beck (Francois Cluzet), a pediatrician under renewed suspicion for the death of his wife, Margot (Marie-Josee Croze), eight years earlier.

In the film's early scenes, the couple -- sweethearts since childhood -- go for a nocturnal skinny-dip. Margot paddles back to the shore first, and Alex hears screams. When he swims to her rescue, an unseen assailant knocks him unconscious into the water, but he survives. She doesn't.

Now, all these years later, two male bodies have been found at the murder scene, prompting the police to reopen the investigation, and take a closer look at Alex.

Alex has allies in his lesbian, horseshow-rider sister, Anne (Marina Hands), Anne's cohabiting partner, Helene (Kristin Scott Thomas), who becomes Alex's best friend, and his lawyer Elysabeth (Nathalie Baye), but he soon finds himself on the run both from the police and some vicious killers.

His only recourse is to turn for aid to local thug Bruno (Gilles Lellouche), who feels indebted to Alex for having recently saved his hemophiliac child.

Alex desperately searches for the evidence that will clear his name, while he tries to make sense of some mysterious videos that have been e-mailed to him that would seem to suggest Margot might still be alive. They end with the injunction to "tell no one."

The surprising denouement -- way more complex but just as talky as that in an Agatha Christie tale -- does include some actions not exactly, shall we say, in accord with Catholic principles, but are more palatable for being basically time-honored elements of the mystery genre. And the film is unusual also in working in aspects of a genuine love story, along with the dirty doings.

Director and co-writer Guillaume Canet (with Philippe Lefebvre) has skillfully adapted American Harlan Coben's novel, set in New York, and was honored with the Cesar award for best director, while Cluzet won the best actor award. The Cesar is the French Oscar.

Cluzet is extraordinary playing a grief-stricken Everyman, and though he's emotionally low-key throughout, his face speaks volumes. There are further superlative performances from Andre Dussollier, Francois Berleand and Jean Rochefort. Canet himself even takes a part.

Some of the violence, sordidness and general thematic material may be too gritty for all tastes -- and the film is certainly an intense workout -- but there's no denying this is the sort of mystery the French do supremely well.

In French, with subtitles.

The film contains brief but brutal violence, some grisly images, murder, suicide, torture, fleeting distant and shadowy nudity, a brief nongraphic sexual encounter, a lesbian relationship, drug use and rough language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
